transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05 14:00 UTC, Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Blake (Head of ML, Nimbus), Samira Khan (Infra), Luis Ortega (CTO)

--- Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be rough) ---
Alex: quick sync to run through the throughput numbers from last week's tuning.

[00:00] Alex: All right hi everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll keep this tight. This is the weekly POC sync for throughput optimization, continuous batching, concurrency targets, queueing, all that fun stuff. Priya and I will run through the results you already shared and then we want to propose the next run.

[00:25] Jordan: Yep thanks, appreciate it. We had the staging run last night, sent logs, hope you got them.

[00:33] Priya: Yep we pulled them in, thanks. We also merged the agent traces so we could look at the end-to-end, and I ran the same synthetic harness you used but with a slightly different arrival pattern to match your traffic burstiness.

[00:48] Samira: Quick note, the staging cluster had a couple node restarts earlier in the week unrelated to the POC, so you might see small blips. I put a note in the spreadsheet.

[01:05] Alex: Good call. Ok Priya take it away on the numbers.

[01:10] Priya: Sure. So baseline before our changes: you were at about 500 rps sustained with p50 around 110ms and p95 around 430ms for the 2k token average prompt. After enabling continuous batching with max batch size 8 and a dynamic batch window of 12ms we saw throughput increase to ~820 rps, p50 dropped to ~95ms, p95 improved to ~320ms, but we saw queueing buildup when concurrent requests exceeded 160.

[01:48] Jordan: When you say queueing buildup, is that request-level queuing inside the Redwood runtime or on the application side?

[01:57] Priya: Mostly inside the runtime dispatcher. We have a small request queue per worker to assemble batches. Under normal load the dispatcher pulls requests and forms batches every 10-20ms. When concurrency spikes above the worker pool capacity, you see the queue depth jump which increases tail latency because requests are waiting to be admitted into a batch.

[02:20] Alex: To be explicit, the tradeoff we tuned for was increasing batching aggressiveness to reduce per-token compute overhead (which improved throughput) but that increases admission latency when you have many in-flight requests. So there's a sweet spot for your traffic pattern.

[02:38] Luis: Right, our traffic tends to be spiky—short bursts with high concurrency for 30-90s. We care more about p95 than average, since customer-facing latencies are service-level agreed on p95.

[02:52] Priya: Understood. For spikey traffic we recommend constraining concurrency at the application layer or using the runtime's soft concurrency limit. We tested two modes: one with higher max batch size (12) and strict batch window 15ms, that gave you 900 rps but p95 went to 380ms on spikes. The other with max batch 6 and 8ms window gave 730 rps but p95 was 270ms and spike behavior was smoother.

[03:28] Samira: What's the memory/kv cache implication of smaller vs larger batches? We saw some GC pressure at the largest settings.

[03:36] Priya: Yeah larger batches increase KV cache write footprint per step because sequences are merged, and longer batch windows keep more KV in-flight. On your instance type (A100-40GB) we saw a 10-15% higher peak memory with batch size 12 vs 6. That aligns with the GC you observed.

[03:58] Jordan: Hmm ok. So from a customer side the immediate ask is: give us the recommended config that hits at least 750 rps while keeping p95 under 350ms in spikey patterns. Can Redwood do that?

[04:12] Alex: Yes, that was our target earlier this week. We believe the recommended starting point is max_batch_size=8, batch_window_ms=12, soft_concurrency_limit=140 per worker, and an application-level queue depth cap of 250 across the cluster. That should give you ~780-820 rps and p95 roughly in the 280-340ms band depending on exact burst shape. We'll include fallbacks (lower batch window) to reduce p95 if you prefer.

[04:45] Luis: When you say soft_concurrency_limit 140 per worker — how many workers in the pool? You need to translate to cluster concurrency.

[04:54] Priya: For your current staging pool of 6 workers that's roughly 840 concurrency target, but the runtime will also do smart routing and rate limit to preserve headroom. We can tie a hard cap at the load balancer if you'd like.

[05:10] Jordan: Is the smart routing redundant with our app-level rate limiter? We need a single source of truth ideally.

[05:17] Alex: Good point, we recommend using app-level throttling as primary and runtime soft limits as secondary to avoid client-side retries thrashing the system. We'll document recommended settings for both.

[05:30] Samira: One more infra question — how does this affect tail latency if a worker goes down and load shifts?

[05:36] Priya: There will be a brief spike while the orchestrator reschedules. We recommend enabling the small warm-up pool or a little buffer capacity to smooth redistrib — Redwood Dedicated supports burst capacity, for the POC we can show a config to keep a hot spare worker.

[05:55] Jordan: Cool. The spreadsheet you sent has a column labeled "k-v chache" spelled weirdly — we think that's KV cache results?

[06:02] Priya: Yeah sorry auto-transcription and my notes — that is KV cache, K-V. Sometimes the agent garbles it.

[06:10] Alex: No worries. Ok let's dive into the percentiles from last night's run. Priya, can you summarize the p50/p95/p99 for the three test configs we kicked off?

[06:20] Priya: Sure. Config A (conservative): batch_size=6, window=8ms, concurrency cap 140 cluster-wide: 730 rps, p50 98ms, p95 270ms, p99 520ms.

[06:36] Priya: Config B (balanced): batch_size=8, window=12ms, soft_concurrency 140 per worker: 800 rps, p50 95ms, p95 320ms, p99 640ms.

[06:52] Priya: Config C (aggressive): batch_size=12, window=15ms, no soft concurrency: 920 rps, p50 88ms, p95 380ms, p99 850ms and noticed queueing spikes when arrival rate spiked over sustained burst.

[07:08] Jordan: Those p99 numbers are a bit alarming for C. We're okay with p99 degradation so long as p95 stays under threshold. For C it's above.

[07:17] Alex: Right so the balanced config B seems like the best compromise. If you expect more spikiness we recommend throttling at the LB or using B but with dynamic window reduction on detected spikes — we have an experimental policy that reduces batch_window_ms by 50% when queue depth > threshold. We can enable that for the staging run.

[07:41] Samira: That dynamic policy — is it safe? Any thrash risk?

[07:45] Priya: It's stateful but tuned to be stable — it works by reducing the wait time for forming a batch, so you trade off some throughput for lower admission latency. It has hysteresis so it doesn't flip frequently. We'll provide recommended hysteresis settings.

[07:59] Luis: Ok if that's safe, let's try it.

[08:02] Alex: Noted. We'll include dynamic window policy in the config we send.

[08:07] Jordan: A couple other items — can you remind us of the cost delta between the configs? Like per token cost or GPU utilization? We need that to weigh tradeoffs.

[08:16] Priya: Sure, rough numbers from the run: Config A GPU utilization ~62%, Config B ~73%, Config C ~88%. Per-token compute cost estimated to be 12% lower in C vs A due to better batching. We'll add a small cost model to the spreadsheet.

[08:31] Jordan: Great. Also on security/compliance — Luis asked offline about logging redaction for PII in the traces, any updates?

[08:40] Alex: Yes we have the redaction settings available; Redwood can redact request bodies at ingest and ship only hashes to the console. We'll attach the SOC2+security doc as a link in the follow-up email.

[08:54] Samira: Please include the exact KMS integration steps; our security team wants key rotation cadence notes.

[09:00] Alex: Will do.

[09:05] Jordan: Back to throughput: we also saw a few 5xxs under config C. Are those from the runtime queue overflow or from the model server OOM?

[09:14] Priya: Those 5xxs we traced — they were worker-side OOMs triggered by a combination of large batch memory footprint and a GC event. We put mitigations in 1) lower max batch size, 2) set conservative per-worker memory cap, 3) bump swap headroom in staging.

[09:33] Alex: We'll include recommended memory caps per model variant given your 40GB A100 hosts.

[09:40] Luis: Regarding model variants — you mentioned smaller quantized variants could help. Tradeoff on quality?

[09:46] Priya: Right we tested a 4-bit quantized candidate; throughput went up ~15% with similar latency, but we did see a small hallucination increase on one of your prompt suites. We'll include a short eval summary. Quantization is an option but requires you to accept slight quality delta.

[10:02] Jordan: We'll review the evals but right now prefer to stay at FP16.

[10:06] Alex: Understood. Ok quick recap of what we're sending: consolidated spreadsheet with raw results + cost model, recommended configs (A/B/C with our pick: B), dynamic batch window policy example, concurrency/queueing JSON snippets, memory cap guidance, and security docs link.

[10:25] Samira: And we'll run the 2-hour sustained test on staging with B + dynamic window, upload logs.

[10:33] Jordan: For the follow-up call on 2026-08-13—can we have one of your SREs on who can help read logs?

[10:40] Alex: Yes I'll include Priya and also add Michael Park (SRE) if available.

[10:45] Priya: Quick technical note: when you run the benchmark, please capture both arrival trace and worker-side dispatcher traces; that makes it easy to correlate queue depth with p95 spikes. We've attached the exact trace commands in the spreadsheet.

[10:58] Luis: Will do.

[11:01] Alex: Any final questions?

[11:05] Jordan: One minor point — can you give us a recommended app-side concurrency cap value? We want a single number to apply.

[11:12] Priya: For your cluster size right now, start with cap = 700 concurrent requests across the cluster. We'll include a lambda to translate that as you scale workers.

[11:22] Alex: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll send the artifacts and next steps by Monday the 9th.

[11:28] Jordan: Thanks - appreciate it.

[11:30] End call.
